title: Total Variation Distance Estimation in Autoregressive Models
claim: Real serving systems behave as noisy oracles whose noise stays small relative to support size, so noise-tolerant estimation is far cheaper than sampling.
layout: 3 panels in a row, left-to-right; bar chart, histogram, line plot
description: Three side-by-side plots with shared model-size legends. Panel (a) is a grouped bar chart of relative standard deviation sigma for five Qwen models (0.6B, 1.7B, 8B, Qwen2.5-7B, 30B MoE) across three attention backends (cuDNN green, FlashAttn-2 orange, math purple). Solid bars show isolated batches and faded full-height bars show served, varying batches. The 30B MoE bars are tallest, at about 0.07 to 0.11. Panel (b) is a log-scale density histogram of single-call log-probability deviations, with sharp peaks at zero and heavier tails for the 30B-MoE curve in red. Panel (c) is a log-log line plot of sigma squared against API top-k from 5 to 100. Most curves fall as k grows, and the red 30B-MoE curve stays flat near 1e-2. The colors are blue and teal shades plus red.
caption: Inference engines as noisy logit oracles. A served model is treated as a per-token logprobability oracle: querying a fixed prefix repeatedly, we measure the relative standard deviation σ of the returned probabilities (σ2 is the relative-variance parameter of Definition 3; five Qwen models, bf16, top-k = 20; calibration in Appendix B.3). (a) σ by attention backend under two batching conditions: isolated (the query alone in a fixed batch; solid) and served (the query batched with other, varying requests, as in production; full bar height). cuDNN is noisy even in isolation; FlashAttention-2 and math are deterministic in isolation and acquire noise only when served. (b) The distribution of single-call log-probability deviations. (c) σ2 against the API top-k truncation: σ2 ≪K throughout, so the noisy-logit bound (n+n2σ2)/ε2 of Theorem 3 is far below the sampling bound n2K/ε2 of Theorem 1.
abstract: Modern LLM deployments use a number of implementation choices and inference optimizations (e.g., batching, custom kernels, and quantization) on top of fixed weights, so two engines serving "the same model" can produce meaningfully different distributions. We study the problem of estimating the total variation (TV) distance between two length-$n$ autoregressive distributions to additive error $\varepsilon$, under three access models. (1) Under sample access, we use $\widetilde{O}(n^2 K/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, where $K$ is the maximum support of the next-token distribution. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^3 m/\varepsilon^5)$-query estimator of Meel et al. (2025), where $m \geq K$ is the total size of the token alphabet. (2) Under logit access, we use $O(n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, and this is tight. (3) Under noisy logit access, we smoothly interpolate between the above two guarantees: if probability values are given to relative error $Ï$, we use $\widetilde{O}((n+n^2Ï^2)/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithms, for example measuring the distance between SGLang and vLLM serving identical weights. Our experiments highlight the robustness and practicality of estimating the total variation distance, which remains estimable where the KL divergence is infinite. Our code is available at https://github.com/XunZhiyang/llm-tv-estimation.
